implementation_notes: Drogon is the direct C++ analogue: app().registerHandler("/orders/{1}", handler) (or an HttpController class) is the controller/dispatcher, the handler calls the service layer, fills an HttpViewData with {{key}} values and answers with HttpResponse::newHttpViewResponse("ShowOrder.csp", data); the CSP template is the view, and its <%c++ %> blocks plus helper functions cover the view-helper slot. What replaces the classic structure is the framework - routing, handler lifecycle and view lookup are library pieces, so only the worker and the template remain yours; the hand-written controller is justified when the project must stay on a bare HTTP library or needs custom dispatch semantics (see the beast-manual-router variant).
pitfalls: HttpViewData is string-keyed: the template's {{order}} and the handler's data.insert("order", ...) agree only at render time, so a rename degrades to an empty placeholder instead of a compile error.
Handlers run on Drogon's event loops - a blocking database call inside one stalls every connection served by that loop; use the async client APIs or a separate thread pool.
Views are enabled/registered explicitly (CSP support at build time, loadView for dynamic cases); a missing template surfaces as a runtime error page, not a build failure.

variants.name: Crow micro-framework with Mustache templates
variants.implementation_notes: Crow keeps the same shape at a smaller scale: CROW_ROUTE(app, "/orders/<int>") registers the worker, which builds a crow::json::wvalue context and returns crow::mustache::load("orders/show.html").render(ctx) - the route table is the dispatcher and the Mustache file is the view. Headers-only and C++11-friendly, so it fits small services and constrained build environments; the classic controller class disappears entirely, which is the point - what remains is worker + template. Choose Drogon instead when the application needs ORM, plugins or an async client stack.
pitfalls: crow::mustache::load resolves against the base path set with crow::mustache::set_base_path - start the binary from another working directory and every view lookup fails at request time.
The context is a hand-built json::wvalue: a key the template does not expect (or lacks) renders an empty section with no diagnostic.
Mustache is logic-less by design - loops and partials only - so anything a template used to compute must be precomputed by the worker.

variants.name: Hand-written dispatcher over a bare HTTP library (Boost.Beast)
variants.idiom_name: std::map<target, handler> route table + render(model) step over Boost.Beast
variants.implementation_notes: With only an HTTP library under you the pattern is hand-written: a std::map (or vector) of {target -> handler} is the controller/dispatcher, each handler returns a model struct instead of markup, and one render function formats that model into the http::response body. This is the variant to choose when the view is produced by your own code or a template engine you already ship, and when matching policy (versioning, custom path rules, content negotiation) must be yours - you pay for it by implementing what a framework would have provided: matching, error mapping and view lookup.
pitfalls: Every route must go through render(); a handler that sets res.body() itself makes the model/template contract unenforceable.
The map lookup provides no wildcards or parameter binding - order-sensitive prefix matching is easy to get wrong and silently serves the wrong page.
Beast's request/response objects are consumed by the asynchronous session stack; copy the model out before serialising so no view reads moved-from state.
